overview: Courts turned back Justice Department efforts over California ballots and election workers, and the department opened a probe tied to a second "Dan Sullivan" on Alaska's Senate ballot, as early voting surges ahead of Tuesday's midterms. Iran said four tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz, Russia's Novaya Gazeta shut down, and Israel's election left no bloc with a majority. On Wall Street, a tech sell-off over AI spending produced the worst day since June, while Fed officials said more rate hikes may be needed. In New York, the City Council took up a bill to create a Department of Community Safety.

stories.headline: Justice Department probes second 'Dan Sullivan' on Alaska Senate ballot
stories.summary: The top federal prosecutor in Alaska confirmed criminal and civil inquiries into the recruitment of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan in the Senate race. The Justice Department also asked a federal judge to have state officials set aside ballots that rank that candidate. Democrat Mary Peltola says she knew nothing about the recruitment.
stories.why_it_matters: The Alaska seat could help decide Senate control, and the court request touches how ballots are counted days before the Nov. 3 election. Coverage splits sharply by outlet lean on whether this is a scheme or a pretext.
stories.background: Alaska's Senate race pits Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan against Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman. A second candidate, Dan J. Sullivan, also qualified for the ballot, and Republicans say Democrats recruited him to confuse voters. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, so a name-alike could draw rankings. The Justice Department sued last week over the matter, and the administration has pushed the case in the closing days of the campaign.

facts.text: The U.S. attorney for Alaska said Friday that federal authorities are investigating whether the Peltola campaign's reported effort to recruit the second candidate violated the law.

In a court filing the Justice Department asked a judge to order that ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan be separated, citing potential voter confusion; NBC noted the filing did not explain how separating ballots would show confusion.
Peltola told supporters Thursday she 'knew nothing' about the recruitment of decoy candidates.
NewsNation reported that running against a candidate who shares your name is not illegal in Alaska or under federal law.
Sen. Lisa Murkowski, a Republican, criticized the Justice Department's lawsuit, according to ABC affiliate reports.

positions.claim: Sen. John Barrasso alleged Sen. Chuck Schumer worked with Peltola's campaign for a year to recruit the candidate.
Peltola says she knew nothing about it.

framing.note: Fox leads with the Republican accusation of a Schumer-backed 'decoy' plot.
NBC leads with the DOJ filing and stresses that it did not explain how separating ballots would show confusion.
The Washington Examiner presents the scheme as established fact and frames it as a pre-election bombshell.
NewsNation focuses on whether the conduct is actually illegal, which others play down.

stories.social: Republicans such as Murkowski have publicly objected to the DOJ suit, while Sullivan's campaign called the matter a Democratic sideshow, per search summaries.

stories.headline: Courts rebuff Justice Department efforts over California ballots and election workers
stories.summary: A federal appeals court rejected, 2-1, the Justice Department's bid to make California set aside mail ballots from over 20,000 people the administration suspects are noncitizens. Separately, a federal judge barred the department from threatening election workers with prosecution for counting those ballots.
stories.why_it_matters: The rulings leave California's vote counting unchanged days before the midterms. They also limit federal pressure on local election officials.
stories.background: The Trump administration alleges that California sent ballots to some 20,000 people who may not be citizens and wants them held until citizenship is verified. California officials dispute this and have resisted. A district court had earlier declined to order the separation, and the Justice Department went to the 9th Circuit. The restraining order came in a lawsuit brought by unions, per The Hill.

facts.text: The 9th Circuit panel voted 2-1 Friday to reject the Justice Department's request for California to set aside the disputed ballots.
U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson issued a temporary restraining order barring the administration from threatening election officials with criminal prosecution over such ballots.
The order says local officials cannot be forced to separate or stop counting ballots the government deems disputed.

framing.note: Axios frames it as a last-minute loss for the Trump DOJ.
The Times highlights the court's description of the idea as plainly unconstitutional.

stories.headline: Christa Pike describes constant pain after failed Tennessee execution
stories.summary: Christa Pike, who survived a lethal injection attempt in Tennessee in September, released her first public statement, saying she is in constant pain and isolated. Her lawyers want her death sentence reduced to life, and the governor has ordered an investigation.
stories.why_it_matters: The case raises questions about how states carry out lethal injections and whether other scheduled executions go forward.
stories.background: Pike was convicted of a 1995 murder and was the first woman executed or scheduled for execution in Tennessee in two centuries. Her execution was attempted by lethal injection at the end of September and did not succeed. Gov. Bill Lee ordered an independent investigation and canceled the state's next scheduled execution, according to local reporting. Her lawyers are asking him to commute her sentence.

facts.text: Pike said in her first public statement since the attempt that she is in constant pain, a month after surviving it.
Her lawyers want her death sentence reduced to life, and the governor has ordered an investigation.
Gov. Lee called for a third-party investigation, canceled the December execution and postponed another; the Corrections commissioner is resigning.

stories.headline: Novaya Gazeta, Russia's best-known independent paper, shuts down
stories.summary: Novaya Gazeta announced on Friday that it is ceasing publication, saying pressure from Russian authorities made its work impossible. The paper was co-founded by a Nobel Peace Prize winner and was among the last outlets openly critical of the Kremlin and the war in Ukraine.
stories.why_it_matters: Fewer independent sources of reporting from inside Russia means less checked information about the war and the government for Russians and for outsiders trying to follow events.
stories.background: Novaya Gazeta was founded in the early 1990s and became known for investigative reporting on corruption, human-rights abuses and the Chechen wars. Several of its journalists have been killed or jailed over the years. Its co-founder Dmitry Muratov shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize. After Russia sent troops into Ukraine in 2022, the Kremlin tightened restrictions on critical media, and the paper's operations were curtailed further.

facts.text: Novaya Gazeta said on Friday it was shutting down, with its editorial team saying authorities forced it to stop work.
The paper had published for more than three decades and was known for investigative journalism.
Its journalists said the state had orchestrated the closure; its founder told the BBC the paper had been 'strangled'.
The Hindu described the closure as a new step in a campaign against dissent that sped up after the 2022 invasion.

stories.headline: Iran says four tankers hit mines and burn in the Strait of Hormuz
stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy said several tankers caught fire after striking mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and Oman rescued 25 sailors from one burning vessel. Reports differ on whether three or four ships were hit, and a US admiral separately said Hormuz mines had been cleared.
stories.why_it_matters: The strait carries a large share of the world's oil, so attacks and halted traffic can raise fuel and shipping costs, and crews, including many from India, are at risk.
stories.background: The war in the region began on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, according to The Hindu. Iran has since restricted shipping through the strait. The US military says it has cleared Iranian mines from international lanes, while Iran's Guards say ships should use channels near its coast and have claimed mine strikes elsewhere. CENTCOM has previously disputed some of those claims.

facts.text: Iran's IRGC Navy said four tankers caught fire in the strait; the AP headline says Iran reported four tankers striking mines.

Reuters cited security sources saying a tanker was hit by limpet mines.

stories.headline: Israel's election leaves neither Netanyahu nor rivals with a majority
stories.summary: Final results gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats and the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot 48, so neither can form a government immediately. Arab-led parties won a combined 19 seats. Netanyahu's party has alleged the election was 'stolen', which AP described as unsubstantiated.
stories.why_it_matters: Weeks of coalition bargaining or another election could delay budgets and policy decisions, and the credit rating agency Fitch cited prolonged political uncertainty in keeping Israel's outlook negative.
stories.background: Israel votes for a 120-seat parliament, and a bloc needs 61 seats to govern. Netanyahu has been prime minister for much of the past two decades. The election was held during a regional war and a long Gaza conflict. Eisenkot, a former military chief, leads the main opposition bloc.

facts.text: Final results: Netanyahu's party and allies won 53 seats, short of a majority; Eisenkot's bloc won 48.
Arab-led parties won a combined 19 seats on record turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Netanyahu's party amplified allegations that Arab-led parties 'stole' the election, possibly with foreign help; AP called them unsubstantiated.
Israeli media reported party members accused Qatar of involvement.
The Washington Times reported the party called the Arab turnout the 'Islamization of Israel'.

stories.headline: Polish police surround top court as president and government clash over its chief
stories.summary: Poland's government suspended the constitutional court's president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and moved toward criminal charges against him and another justice. Riot police stood outside the court and three protesters were detained; President Karol Nawrocki cut short a trip to Africa and backs the suspended judge.
stories.why_it_matters: The dispute is about who controls Poland's highest court, which affects how laws are checked, and it comes amid a wider tension between the government and the president.
stories.background: Poland's constitutional court has been contested since the previous nationalist government changed how judges were appointed. Prime Minister Donald Tusk's centrist government says it is restoring the rule of law, while President Nawrocki, a nationalist, rejects the suspensions. The sides disagree on who holds legitimate judicial appointments.

facts.text: Tusk defended the firing of court president Swieczkowski as a move to 'restore the rule of law'.
The government suspended two senior justices and moved to bring criminal charges.

stories.headline: Binance says hackers took about $6.3 billion in record crypto theft
stories.summary: Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, said a security breach affected about $6.3 billion in assets and that it will cover customer losses. Roughly $3 billion has been frozen so far, and the exchange paused withdrawals. Suspicion has fallen on North Korean hackers, though the White House says it does not yet know.
stories.why_it_matters: Millions of people keep money on exchanges like Binance, and the company's pledge to cover losses is what protects them here. The theft also puts renewed pressure on regulators and on the security practices of crypto platforms.
stories.background: Binance is the largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume, founded by Changpeng Zhao. Crypto exchanges hold customers' coins in wallets they control, which makes them targets for large thefts. North Korean state-linked hackers have been tied by researchers to several earlier large crypto thefts. Stablecoin issuers such as Circle and Tether can freeze their own tokens, which is how part of the stolen money was frozen. The size of this theft is far above earlier records, according to AP and other outlets.

facts.text: Binance said a security breach affected about $6.3 billion in assets, and that roughly $3 billion has been frozen and losses will be covered.
Outlets including AP, NPR and the Financial Times describe it as the largest crypto theft on record.

The Financial Times reports Binance said an engineer's laptop was compromised in the breach.
The Wall Street Journal reports the loss exceeded the funds the exchange had set aside to cover such an incident.
Binance co-founder said the exchange does not need to sell its SpaceX shares to cover losses, per Reuters.
A US State Department spokesman called North Korean cybercrime a "global problem".

positions.claim: A research lab attributed the theft to North Korea's elite hacking unit, and several outlets name North Korea as the prime suspect.
President Trump said the administration is looking into it and "we don't know" whether North Korea is responsible.

stories.headline: Tech sell-off over AI spending gives Wall Street its worst day since June
stories.summary: The S&P 500 fell 1.8% on Friday, its worst day since June, and closed a third straight losing week as investors questioned returns on heavy AI spending. Disappointing earnings from Amazon, Alphabet and Intel drove the declines, and the Nasdaq dropped about 3% at one point. Intel had its worst day in decades.
stories.why_it_matters: Big tech stocks make up a large share of most retirement and index funds, so a prolonged drop in them shows up in 401(k) balances. Worries that the AI spending boom may not pay off also bear on the companies hiring and investing across the economy.
stories.background: Large technology companies have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to AI data centers and chips over the past two years, and stock prices rose on expectations of large future profits. This month investors began to question how quickly that spending can earn returns. Several of the biggest firms reported quarterly results this week. Some have also drawn credit-rating scrutiny over their borrowing, with S&P revising Meta's outlook to negative.

MarketWatch attributes Intel's slide to pressure on its PC business as memory-chip prices dent demand and corporate IT budgets shrink.
BBC reports Google's value fell by about $500 billion after it said its AI search summaries were affecting ad revenue.
S&P Global revised Meta's credit outlook to negative over capital spending and free cash flow, per Reuters.
The Financial Times reports that revelations Anthropic could receive a junk credit rating after its IPO added to concerns over industry borrowing.

stories.headline: Exxon and Chevron beat estimates as oil industry profits surge during Iran war
stories.summary: ExxonMobil and Chevron reported third-quarter results that beat forecasts, helped by high oil prices, record production and strong refining margins. The New York Times and New York Post both report US oil and gas companies earned more than $130 billion during the war. The results land as drivers face high gasoline and diesel prices.
stories.why_it_matters: High fuel prices raise costs for commuters, truckers and anyone buying goods that are shipped. The profits are also a political issue days before the midterms.
stories.background: The US is at war with Iran, and attacks on refineries in the Middle East and Russia have tightened global fuel supplies. That pushed up crude oil and especially diesel prices. Oil companies that refine fuel have earned larger margins as a result. President Trump has both touted the benefits of high oil prices and, per CNBC, said Big Oil was making too much money.

stories.headline: City Council takes up bill to create a Department of Community Safety
stories.summary: The City Council debated a bill on Friday that would create a Department of Community Safety, a signature promise of Mayor Zohran Mamdani. The mayor's existing Office of Community Safety also made its case to lawmakers, with its commissioner saying it works in constant contact with the NYPD.
stories.why_it_matters: The outcome shapes who responds to some mental health and quality-of-life calls in the city, and how much money moves toward that work. Only left-leaning and center outlets in the digest covered the hearing.
stories.background: Mayor Mamdani campaigned on creating a city department focused on community safety and mental health response. After taking office he set up an Office of Community Safety by executive order, as a step before a full department. A bill to make a department in law was introduced by Council Member Lincoln Restler and referred to the Government Operations committee. NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch remains in her post, and the office says it is separate from the police but coordinates with them.

stories.headline: Upper West Side barn owl nest damaged by rooftop work; state looks into it
stories.summary: The roof of a water tower on an Upper West Side building, where a family of barn owls had nested, was removed this week. Birders were angry, and conservation officers arrived at the site.
stories.why_it_matters: Barn owls are protected, and the case tests how construction rules are enforced when wildlife is involved in a dense neighborhood.
stories.background: In October a family of barn owls was found nesting in a water tower atop a building on West 75th Street near Central Park. An expert quoted by the AP called it the first documented barn owl nesting in Manhattan in modern history. Nightly crowds gathered to watch. The state Department of Environmental Conservation says the species has declined sharply in New York, and Gothamist notes the birds are protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act.

stories.headline: Council leaders favor expanding Fair Fares over free buses
stories.summary: At a City & State event, Council Speaker Julie Menin and Majority Leader Shaun Abreu said widening eligibility for Fair Fares is the best way to address transit affordability, rather than making buses free.
stories.why_it_matters: Fare policy affects what low-income riders pay each day. The position signals the Council's preference as free buses remain a mayoral campaign theme. This was covered by a single outlet.
stories.background: Fair Fares is a city program that gives half-price MetroCards or OMNY discounts to eligible low-income New Yorkers. Free buses were a key campaign promise of Mayor Mamdani. The Council controls much of the city budget that would pay for either approach. Menin and Abreu lead the Council.

stories.headline: NYCHA says it removed asbestos residue at Marcy Houses
stories.summary: NYCHA officials say white dust on residents' windows at the Marcy Houses in Bedford-Stuyvesant came from steam from a mobile boiler line's exhaust vent, and that the asbestos-containing residue has been removed.
stories.why_it_matters: Residents of public housing want to know whether their homes are safe, and the claim of removal rests on NYCHA's own statement. Only Gothamist in the digest covered it.
stories.background: NYCHA runs the city's public housing and has had repeated problems with heat and boilers. Temporary mobile boilers are sometimes used when heating plants are down. Asbestos is a mineral that can harm lungs if fibers are inhaled. Marcy Houses is a complex in Bedford-Stuyvesant.

concept.explanation: The Consumer Price Index tracks what a typical basket of goods and services costs, such as food, rent, gasoline and medical care, and the headline number is how much that basket cost compared with a year earlier. It reaches your wallet through everyday prices and through the Fed: when inflation runs hot, the Fed can raise interest rates, which makes mortgages, car loans and credit cards more expensive.
